rich_summary: Book 8 of the Mahabharata (Karna‑parva) opens after the death of Drona, when the Kaurava camp is shaken by grief and fear. Duryodhana appoints Karna as the new commander, hoping his prowess will turn the tide against the Pandavas. Karna leads a devastating assault for two days, slaughtering many warriors, yet the long‑awaited duel with Arjuna ends in Karna’s death. The narrative then shifts to Hastinapura, where Sanjaya reports the catastrophe to the blind king Dhritarashtra. Overwhelmed, the king laments the fall of his greatest champions—Bhishma, Drona, Karna, and many princes—recognizing too late that his earlier choices and rejected counsel led to the ruin of his dynasty. The chapter emphasizes fate, regret, and the tragic consequences of pride and war.

highlight_spans.why: The epic’s opening title signals the transition into the Karna‑parva, one of the most tragic phases of the war.
The formal invocation and beginning frame the narrative as sacred history told within layered storytelling.
The introductory lines establish the epic context and ritual invocation before recounting the catastrophic events following Drona’s death.
The opening passage symbolically marks the solemn tone of the book, foreshadowing grief, loss, and the fall of great warriors.

top_scenes.scene_text: Karna, blazing with fury on his chariot, releases dense swarms of arrows like clouds of bees while the armies clash beneath dust and banners.
In the palace of Hastinapura, the blind king Dhritarashtra collapses to the floor as the royal women cry out after hearing of Karna’s death.
Sanjaya solemnly recounts the long list of fallen warriors before the grieving king, the hall dim and filled with mourning courtiers.
